introduction-the-copilot-era.core: LLM assistants (Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT and IDE agents) can draft Terraform, Kubernetes and policy code in seconds, shifting the engineer's role from writer to reviewer. They are excellent at boilerplate and recall of common patterns, but they predict plausible text, not verified truth. So everything they produce still has to pass the same validation, scanning, plan review and testing as human code.

first_principles.problem: A team adopts AI coding and doubles output, but also doubles the number of misconfigured resources reaching review.

analogy.title: A fast junior engineer who never says 'I don't know'
analogy.story: They produce a lot quickly and confidently, so every piece needs a senior review.
analogy.breaks: Juniors learn from feedback; base models don't remember your corrections.

example.title: Writer to reviewer
flow: Prompt: 'S3 bucket with KMS and access logs'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Minutes instead of an hour, with the same checks.

check.q: Why must AI-generated IaC pass the same checks as human code?
check.a: LLMs produce plausible but sometimes wrong or insecure code, and only validation, scanning and review catch it.

prompt-engineering-for-iac.core: Output quality tracks prompt quality. Effective IaC prompts state the tool and version (Terraform 1.9, AWS provider 5.x), the exact resources and constraints (encryption, no public access, tags), the house conventions (module structure, naming), and the desired output format (files, variables with validation, outputs). Supplying examples of your existing modules as context dramatically improves fit.

first_principles.problem: 'Create an S3 bucket' returns deprecated inline ACLs and no encryption.
truths: Models fill gaps with generic defaults.

analogy.title: Briefing a contractor
analogy.story: 'Build a shed' gets you anything; a spec with materials, dimensions and building codes gets what you need.
analogy.breaks: Contractors ask clarifying questions; models often just guess.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Output close to production standard on first try.

code.text:
Terraform >= 1.9, hashicorp/aws ~> 5.60.
Create a module 'secure_bucket':
- aws_s3_bucket + separate aws_s3_bucket_* resources (no inline ACLs)
- SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key passed as variable kms_key_arn
- Block all public access; enforce TLS via bucket policy
- Required tags: owner, cost-center (validate non-empty)
- Outputs: bucket_id, bucket_arn
Files: main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf. Follow the style of the example below.
<example module here>

check.q: Why include provider versions in an IaC prompt?
check.a: Resource schemas change between versions; without them, models often emit deprecated or invalid arguments.

scaffolding-modules-and-policies.core: LLMs are strongest at beating the blank page: generating a module skeleton (versions.tf, variables with descriptions and validation, outputs, README, examples), converting between formats (CloudFormation to Terraform, YAML to cdk8s), drafting Rego or Checkov policies from plain-language rules, and writing test scaffolds. The engineer then refines the logic, the part that needs real judgement.

first_principles.problem: Writing a new module's variables, docs and tests takes a day before any real logic is written.
derivation: Draft **policies** from rules in plain English.

analogy.title: Scaffolding on a building site
analogy.story: It goes up fast and gives structure, but the real walls are built and inspected by the crew.
analogy.breaks: Scaffolding comes down; generated code stays, so it must be cleaned up.

steps.label: Review
steps.detail: Human notices the second rule should also be prod-only, or not, and decides.

code.text:
# Rule: 'RDS instances in prod must be Multi-AZ and encrypted'
package terraform.rds
import rego.v1

deny contains msg if {
  some rc in input.resource_changes
  rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
  rc.change.after.tags.env == "prod"
  not rc.change.after.multi_az
  msg := sprintf("%s must be Multi-AZ", [rc.address])
}

deny contains msg if {
  some rc in input.resource_changes
  rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
  not rc.change.after.storage_encrypted
  msg := sprintf("%s must be encrypted", [rc.address])
}

check.q: Which part of module development should remain human-led?
check.a: Design decisions, business logic and edge cases, which require context and judgement the model lacks.

the-dark-side-hallucinations-and-drift.core: LLMs confidently invent things: arguments that don't exist, resource types from other providers, outdated syntax (inline S3 ACLs, aws_s3_bucket_object), and insecure defaults copied from old tutorials. Beyond hallucinations, generated code can drift from your organisation's standards and duplicate modules you already have. Some fake package or module names are even registered by attackers (slopsquatting).

first_principles.problem: An AI-suggested module source points to a lookalike registry module that an attacker published.
truths: Training data includes old and insecure code.
derivation: Check against **org standards** and existing modules.

analogy.title: A confident tour guide who makes up history
analogy.story: It sounds right and fluent, but some 'facts' are fabricated, and you only find out by checking.
analogy.breaks: Fake history is harmless; fake modules can run code in your pipeline.

code.text:
$ terraform validate
Error: Unsupported argument
  on main.tf line 4, in resource "aws_s3_bucket" "b":
   4:   encryption_enabled = true
An argument named "encryption_enabled" is not expected here.

check.a: Attackers registering package or module names that LLMs commonly hallucinate, so blindly used suggestions pull malicious code.

building-a-safe-ai-assisted-iac-workflow.core: A safe AI-assisted workflow keeps humans and automation in the loop. The AI drafts in the IDE with org context; pre-commit runs fmt, validate, tflint and Checkov; the PR shows the plan, policy results and cost; a human reviews intent and design; apply happens only via the pipeline. Label AI-assisted changes, restrict module sources, and never give agents direct apply credentials.

first_principles.problem: An AI agent with cloud credentials applies a generated change directly and deletes a production subnet.

analogy.title: A sous-chef who preps but doesn't serve
analogy.story: They chop and prepare fast; the head chef tastes and plates before anything leaves the kitchen.
analogy.breaks: Sous-chefs know the kitchen; AI needs context fed explicitly.

example.title: Pipeline
flow: Engineer prompts AI with module examples

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: AI speed with full safety net.

check.q: Why shouldn't AI coding agents hold infrastructure apply credentials?
check.a: Their mistakes would reach production directly; keeping apply in the reviewed pipeline preserves the safety net.
